utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'd like us to go into private session so that I can discuss a particular matter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, can I just put a question to you while we wait? I understood you to say that the three witnesses which we have mentioned are to be offering evidence through 92 bis. That is to say that they will not appear in court. And in that case, we -- in that case, a pseudonym would be sufficient to protect their identity. But the question is then: Do you anticipate that any of them might appear for cross-examination under 92 ter?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the three witnesses are in the group of witnesses to come under Rule 92 bis, and, of course, we even envisaged the possibility under Rule 92 bis to have them appear, all the same. This is the reason why we are going to comply with your order, and you are going to receive supplemental information so that you can rule as to the protective measures for the three witnesses. So we quite understood, fully understood, this possibility; that is, that further to your order, under Rule 92 bis, you could decide that the witnesses should appear before you. In such an event there would be face distortion and that might be then a topical matter. And this is what we are going to do. We are going to comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are waiting for the witness. The court deputy is checking on the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are being updated on the problem of the appearance of the witness. The witness has not been found in any of the rooms where he should be. This has been reported to the Victims and Witnesses Unit, and also, I believe, to the security. If the witness is not here within a reasonable time, we would move to the next witness. Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course this is how it has to be. However, as far as we were informed yesterday, this witness has to be picked up from the hotel at 4:00 p.m. That was the plan for yesterday with the Victims and Witnesses Unit. So according to this service's plan, his witness is supposed to be where he is going to be picked up at 4.00 p.m. However, he may already be here, but anyway, we will have to wait for him and it will all depend on how this is going to be organised and arranged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we have been told that he has been found and will be here in a few minutes. So we'll have an exercise in patience, in waiting. But I must say I didn't understand Mr. Tapuskovic's assertion that the witness was to be picked up at 4.00 p.m. Oh, it's the next witness you're talking about, the next witness? I see. Okay. [Microphone not activated] ... something might happen which might require that the other witness be present. It seems to me that they should have two witnesses here at any given time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To keep you updated, the court deputy has just informed me that the vehicle transporting the witness has just arrived. So our wait may end in another three or four minutes. As an indication of how long we have been waiting, you might have noticed that the security guards have changed positions. They do that every half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please sit, Mr. Elez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before the examination-in-chief continues, Mr. Elez, you owe the Court an explanation as to why you're late. You should have been here for 2.15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The appointment was made for me that way. I waited in the lobby of the hotel at quarter to 2.00. Nobody came to pick me up, so at 2.10, 2.15 I made a call to find out what was going on, why nobody was there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When were you picked up? What time were you picked up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have a watch but I believe it was 20 past 2.00, and the traffic was jammed, as far as I could see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What -- where are you staying? Well, don't answer that. Don't answer that. But that would have to be done in private session. But I'm going to have the court deputy bring this matter to the attention of the registrar so that a full report explaining the late arrival of the witness is made to the Court tomorrow. Proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday we started the examination-in-chief, and now I have to cover a few general matters that did not seem topical for the Defence yesterday. I would like to ask you, at the moment when you joined the army of Republika Srpska, had there been any proclamations from any side about joining various armies?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On TV and on the radio there were announcements. Late Mr. Alija Izetbegovic called on all able-bodied men to join the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I could not join that army because I didn't belong there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about the population of Grbavica? Were there any calls made on them from the other side?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The other side also proclaimed a mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please explain to the Judges -- you have already stated what your relations were with members of other ethnic communities. When the conflict broke out, what was your attitude to members of other ethnic communities, if there were any around you at the time of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Grbavica, interethnic relations were normal. In entranceways, even in buildings, even joint guard duty was organised between Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you understood me. That was before the conflict. Now we are talking about the time when the conflict already broke out. At the outset, were Muslims subjected to any unpleasantries? How did you treat members of other ethnic communities, I don't know, Croats, Muslims, maybe, gypsies, if there were any.

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the Muslims had crossed over to the other side of the Miljacka river. Many Croats had joined the army of Republika Srpska. Some Muslims who stayed on with their families did not want to accept rifles, although a couple of them did. I know that they helped unload or distribute humanitarian aid. In other words, they performed the kinds of work for which they were able.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wonder if we might have the basis of the witness's knowledge of these fairly general statements that he is making. It's always possible that I've missed something but so far I have heard the witness say that he lived in Grbavica at a particular flat, that he joined the army, and that other than a brief stint as a platoon leader, he served in a trench as a private along the Miljacka river, and yet the witness is giving general statement about the -- general statements, excuse me, about the behaviour of entire ethnic communities and I just don't see the basis for him to be able to make these statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us ask him, then. Witness, what is the basis for the statements that you have just made? How did you acquire that knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Presiding Judge, I was an eyewitness to some of the developments, not all, but from what I was able to see, I can speak about my immediate neighbourhood. I know what my neighbours in my building did, or people in the building next door. That is how I made my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Anything further, Mr. Docherty, I think you'll have to take up in cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. And only after cross-examination will I perhaps come back to this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in picking up on one of the things you said. When was your second child born?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: My second child was born in November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So -- thank you. That will be enough. And at the time of the Dayton Accords, what happened with you, your family, your mother?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Dayton Accords were concluded, Grbavica fell under the federation. We did not dare to stay because we had the threats issued over the mass media. Not a single soldier dared to stay on with his family. We left our homes and we left that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you joined the army of Republika Srpska, as you explained the last time, who were the people who made up your unit in the location which you described last time?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my unit, most of the troops were local people from town, and I knew them. There were also some people who had crossed over from the other side, from neighbourhoods such as Pofalici. Some of them left their families back on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know when General Dragomir Milosevic took over command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Dragomir Milosevic took over command in August 1994. I remember that because sanctions were imposed at that time by Serbia and Montenegro, and humanitarian aid stopped coming or continued in a trickle. Neither the people nor the army had much food.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you explain to the court who at that time occupied the positions on the confrontation line between the two armies while General Milosevic was the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who were the soldiers, the fighting men, who made up the unit to which you belonged at the time when General Dragomir Milosevic took over command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit that was on the other bank of the Miljacka river was called, I believe, King Tvrtko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please. All right. I'm not going to interrupt you. What did you mean when you said that the King Tvrtko unit was on the other side?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: That unit was positioned there only then, at the end of 1994. We found that out when they started crossing over to our side. A couple of soldiers from that unit crossed over to our side. We had a report about that. Out of 56 soldiers who were on that line, left -- abandoned their rifles the next day and crossed over to our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And they were from which ethnic community, the soldiers of that King Tvrtko unit?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I actually meant to ask you was who were the fighting men in that platoon, in the company, at the moment when General Dragomir Milosevic took over command? Who were the men in your own unit?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the same soldiers as in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we see again for a moment the map that was on the screens at the end of the previous session? I would later like to save that map and ask two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this the map on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I meant the photograph of the city. Last time I asked our learned friend Shawn to keep it handy. It was actually a photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us see whether he has complied with your request.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, last time you gave us all the explanations to accompany these markings. Could you explain the Trial Chamber once again, at the time when General Milosevic took over command and you were on those confrontation lines, as you described, what were the activities on that confrontation lines when you were there? What was going on?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our army, marked in red, was along the Miljacka river in residential buildings, on the ground floor, and we were additionally protected by sandbags, and we were facing the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the other side. We don't see the flanks here on this picture, but on the flanks, they were positioned in private homes. They were all fortified. Grbavica is situated in a depression, like in a pot. It was surrounded on all sides and there was only one way out, the road via Vrace that went uphill and it was constantly under fire. Grbavica was under fire from Debelo Brdo, Mojmilo hill, Hrasno, Pero Kosoric, a neighbourhood, from high-rise buildings, from the top of the Energoinvest building, the building we called Sibicara, from the science school of the university. We don't see here the building of the Executive Council, but they had positions even there. And the entire area was covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say fire was coming among other sources from Debelo Brdo. If we look at this position, what does that mean? You were facing Miljacka river. What does it mean fire coming from Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Troops of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were on Debelo Brdo. They were behind our backs, if we were in Grbavica, just as they were on Mojmilo hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did anything happen to you personally during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994, troops were being concentrated, troops of the ABH, in locations around Sarajevo such as central Trnovo, and in 1994, I was in a place called Polom, where I was wounded on the 24th September 1994, by a mortar shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How long were you out of combat due to that injury?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on sick leave for 45 days, and after that I went again to Polom. And the same locations as before. We had to assist the Ozrenska unit because strong forces were concentrated around Sarajevo. At that time there were no major attacks against Grbavica but there were attacks on other surrounding locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: For how long -- how long did you have to be in Prolom and in other locations that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: That lasted until end December 1994, when there was a cease-fire, until May 1995. We observed the cease-fire. Perhaps there were individual violations, like in March, the killing of two girls by soldiers of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who shot at the two girls from the direction of --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. We've heard about that. But tell me, did you ever meet General Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was in the spring of 1995, when commander Dragomir Milosevic was touring the forward defence lines. I was at the time in my position next to the Miljacka river, and at that time, he addressed the troops staying, "Take care of yourselves, boys. If you have survived this long, hold on a bit longer." And then he said, "There were reports on television citing civilian casualties and saying that somebody is shooting at the civilians" and I said to the commander, "We can't see a thing from here. We rarely see even a soldier running across, and there can be no civilians here. This area is an area where there are only business, office buildings, and anyway, we would never shoot at civilians because we all have families. And even on the other side, many of us have families who stayed there, immediate family or more distant family. So it's nobody from our side who is shooting."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was it possible for anyone to cross over from one side to another? I'm talking about civilians.

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grbavica was rather constrained. There weren't any broad lines. Some attempts were made across the Miljacka. I didn't see that. I heard about that. And these attempts ended in the Miljacka. Also, near Zeljeznicar stadium, two other streets -- well, the street is not very wide, so people would run across there. So quite a few people tried to cross over to the other side. Some succeeded, others didn't. And those who did cross over talked about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to tell you -- I would like to show you a document, actually. That is DD003028 -- or 3208, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whilst the document is being retrieved, I would like to ask a question of the witness. Witness, you said that when General Milosevic advised you not to shoot at civilians, and also to take care of yourselves, you said you answered to the commander that there were no civilians around and that anything -- anyway, nothing was happening there. When you say "commander," did you mean General Milosevic himself or did you say that to your own commander of your own unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the answer that I gave to commander Dragolub [as interpreted] Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Personally, you spoke to him personally, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, to him personally, because as I've already said, I happened to be there on the positions as he was touring them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. Very well, but please answer this question, and it's my last question: There were no military activities? In other words, your unit was not shooting, it was not firing any shells or anything of that type?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While the cease-fire was on, no gunfire was opened. We fully observed the cease-fire. It was easier for us, too, when it was that kind of situation, when there were no casualties. We thought that in that way the war had stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How frequently did General Milosevic tour the positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how frequently he toured the positions. I saw him then. I heard that he did tour the positions but I did not happen to come across him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You saw him only once, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Elez, please take a look at this document. It's a bit blurred but this is the form that I found it in. Could you please have a look and see who it was that issued this document? Please look at the date. Please look at what the heading says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It should be enlarged. Can it be enlarged? Because it's difficult it read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I can see it. I think I can see what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you can, could you read out the letterhead and the heading first?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Army unit 5454." The date is the 15th of October 1994. I think it says, "Combat report to the commander of the 101st Motorised Brigade."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now please take a look at paragraph 2, that says, "Our forces"? And could you have a look at it and what is it that happened at 2015 hours?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it. Is it necessary for me to read it out?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At 2015 hours, our guard, who is at Palma noticed an escapee who tried to escape to the aggressor's side. He opened fire and on that occasion he wounded him."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that the kind of thing that happened, that you heard of, and that you have not seen, as you said, when somebody would try to cross over to the other side where the army of Republika Srpska was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty is on his feet. Mr. Docherty?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, again the witness has no basis for answering this question and counsel as much as conceded that in the way he put his question: Is that the kind of thing that happened, that you heard of, that you have not seen? I mean, we should be hearing from witnesses with firsthand knowledge, if at all possible, and I object to a witness looking at a document from not even his own military unit, indeed from the opposing side, and then generalising on the basis of that document to things that he apparently has no firsthand knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We do take in hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I realise that, Your Honour. I'm not objecting on the grounds that it's hearsay. I'm objecting on the grounds that it's not reliable, and I think that Rule 89(C), although it gives Trial Chambers very broad discretion, does say that Trial Chambers may take into -- may admit into evidence any reliable evidence, and I put it that this question is calling for unreliable evidence by asking the witness about things that he has heard but not seen. We doesn't know from whom. We don't know how reliable the source is. The source is not here. I cannot cross-examine the source and subject their evidence to the test of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a feature of all hearsay evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour in this particular case it goes to the reliability. I've made my submission, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I respond? First, I asked the witness what he knew about such matters, and he said very nicely that there were places where one could cross over but that this kind of thing would happen and this is what I asked him before I showed him the document. Then I showed him the document. I did expand on the question, that is true, in the spirit of what the Prosecutor just said, but he said even before I showed him this document that this kind of thing happened. My next question to him would be, to have it sound even more convincing, I think that he can answer this, where was this facility that is referred to here, Palma? From the place where he was, could he see that facility or at any rate, did he know where Palma was, from where the guard opened fire, as is written here, and hit the man who was trying to escape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us proceed on the basis, then, that you will ask the witness from where he was could he see Palma. So I'll ask the witness that. From where you were, could you see Palma?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not see Palma from where I was because Palma is by the Zeljeznicar stadium, Grbavica number 2, by the Loris building, Zeljeznicar stadium, that is to say, where Strojorad is. I know full well where the building is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe you didn't understand what he said. He said Palma is by the Loris building. Did you hear that? Did you hear him say that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is your next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, could the Loris building be seen from that location, from the place where he lived and where he moved about most of the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ask him the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you answer that question? You said Palma was by the Loris building. How tall was Palma? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the place where I was, where my apartment was, where the position was, one could not fully see the Loris building or Palma, for that matter, but behind the Palma building, one could see high skyscrapers, four skyscrapers. Then also a square called Pero Kosoric square. From these skyscrapers, you can see enough. I can tell you about a particular case that happened. Dusan Karan, an officer, stayed on there. He lived there. He was an elderly man, 70 years old, a retired officer of the Yugoslav army. He is the father of my brother-in-law. One of his sons lived there in Sarajevo. It was established that somebody shot that man and killed him, from those skyscrapers, on their side. They ascribed this killing to us. The post-mortem established that we were the not ones -- we were not the ones who were shooting but that they were shooting from their side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about these -- such cases that, like the one described here? Were they ascribed also to the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many who were on the other side, on the other bank of the Miljacka in Sarajevo and who happened to cross over, sometimes through an exchange, cross over to our side, or something like that, they talked and there were stories going around to the effect that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, when there were mass gatherings or regularly when people went to fetch water, the army placed explosive devices, which resulted in casualties among the civilian population and then they blamed us. I don't know. I was not an eyewitness, but there were a lot of stories that were told about that kind of thing. As Markale was described too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's not what I asked you. How many such cases were there according to your knowledge, cases like the one described in this document?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several cases. I don't know the actual names involved but quite a few things like that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document, well, I'd like to tender it as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D216, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we try to wrap this up now? Actually, first, Your Honours, [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Tapuskovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The photograph, the photograph disappeared again, the one that we took while the document was displayed. However, I hear from the representative of the Registry that it's still around and that it can be kept as a Defence Exhibit too.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this photograph that was marked by the witness was admitted as D215 yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Elez, can you tell us now, after the period that you described to us just now, the period that was more quiet, when there was a cease-fire, when did the conflict break out again?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the summer of 1995, I think it was June or July, there were more frequent attacks coming from the flanks of Grbavica. That is to say from Miska Jovanovica, Beogradska, Ljubljanska, Ozrenska street, then from the Mojmilo hill, attacks at Djukica Potok.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did this escalate, though? When was all of this displayed to a large extent? When?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could notice that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was better armed because they fired at us more often and with more ammunition, gunfire, artillery at all fronts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. However, when was this particularly pronounced, if we are speaking in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: June, July, August. I'm talking about months now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember all the details about the period after that. I know that there were attacks on all fronts, such as Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You've said enough. You mentioned the street of Miska Jovanovica and then Investbanka and some other street. Now, I'd like to show you a document. This document, does it correspond to what you were describing until now, the attacks coming from the flanks and so on and so forth, all the things you said? The document is DD002614. Mr. Elez, can you please look at the letterhead, the date and what is written immediately below the letterhead? And can you please read it?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: "12th Division command, Sarajevo, the 1st of July 1995. Interim combat report on our attacks, BD, combat operations, on the Grbavica axis."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you first look at item B, which begins with the words, "On" --

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At about 1120 hours on the 1st of July 1995, after provocation action by our snipers, and assets on Zagrebacka street".

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Can you also please look at what is described under item A, at the beginning? If you can read that because minutes ago you mentioned a street. Does this correspond to what you said?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 20th of June 1995, JG 4/115 consisting of eight officers and men mounted a strike against the probably combat sector of the aggressor on Miska Jovanovica street, corner of Ivana Gorana Kovacica street, conducting -- "

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Can you also take a look at this paragraph which begins, "On" and then there is a date, the first number is 26?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 26th of June 1995, the 4/115 BBR, POS targeted A 8 BBT of the aggressor in the butcher's, the Investbanka and the red building in order to distract and tie up the aggressor and to mount a surprise attack on the facility that the assault group 4/115 BBR had temporarily occupied on the 20th of June 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this consistent with what you were telling us a minute ago about the attacks from the flanks and incursions in your territory? Does this correspond to what you said spontaneously a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of who knows how many incursions? Maybe a 50th incursion by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the flanks, as I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this document, DD002614 be admitted into evidence as a Defence Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D217, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you already mentioned this and described, there is another document, number DD003542, and I would like to you confirm if this document also corroborates what you said.

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please wait a little bit? It's not up yet. Witness, please, now you have it. Can you first look at the letterhead, the date and the issuing party of this document?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, army General Staff, number 1/825-1059, date 11th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we scroll it a bit up and can you tell me who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was signed and stamped by Army General Rasim Delic. That's his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now read paragraph 1 that you can see, the whole of it you can see on the screen, and then we shall quickly finish with this.

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Up to the 15th of July -- "

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, please, the first paragraph, beginning with, "Considering."

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. "Considering that we have entered into the fourth year of war against Serbia and Montenegrin aggressor and in the stage of liberation of PZT, and that types of combat actions well known to us, frontal combined and partisan do not always use adequately and according to the existing situation, and present experiences show -- " I cannot see exactly -- "that partisan type of combat action within the same, we use very little, although the arrangement of our forces, particularly characteristics of the terrain enables that, and for the purpose of intensifying the partisan type of combat actions, active actions, and particularly combat action diversions, I hereby order."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now look what is written under item 4 and can you please read that out?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: "These tasks to be realised as frequent as possible and as deep as possible, to PZT, and create with the enemy as great as possible insecurity. Actions to be taken according to the system, destroy and come back."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this correspond to what you said earlier, also with regard with the previous document, and what you described in your evidence here?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document fully corresponds to all my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this document be admitted as a Defence Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What are you asking us to draw from this document, Mr. Tapuskovic, in particular, paragraph 4? What are you asking us to say that this document illustrates, so far as your case is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the time that involves the most important counts from the indictment, i.e. June and July, so if you look at the indictment, you could see that the majority of incidents happened in June and July. The witness explained here before you how these activities looked like in that period, and this is the best document relating to the things that were dominant in that period and which inevitably gave rise to the necessity regarding these incursions written in block letters, destroy and come back, destroy and come back. Therefore, it was impossible not to respond to these actions. And if you were to examine the whole document, that was the period when the most difficult things were happening in this conflict. These combat operations were conducted on a daily basis and they inevitably led to certain difficulties and hardships for everyone living there. I'm not going to separate civilians and soldiers at all. Ergo, this demonstrates to what extent the responses by the army of Republika Srpska were unavoidable because it was impossible not to respond to a sabotage action, precisely as it says here, to cause provocation and to be active elsewhere on the front during the fiercest offensive. So this shows to the highest possible extent the necessity of responses that the army of Republika Srpska did. And a necessary response to a certain action under international law is permissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're saying that the charges in the indictment that relate to this period, in fact illustrate the responsive character of the Serb attacks?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The necessity of responding to numerous sabotage actions based on a very simple principle: Destroy and come back. It was impossible not to respond to it. There is not a single army anywhere in the world that would refrain from responding to this. They had to devote their attention to these actions rather than to shoot at civilians from hills. And this remains to be seen whether there were any incidents of direct shooting by the army of Republika Srpska, deliberately targeting the civilians or whether this was the period that was one of the most difficult ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You might also want to make something of the sentence, "And create with the enemy as great as possible insecurity." You might want to suggest that this goes to the question of terror insecurity, and that so far as the terror charge is concerned in the indictment, that this is an indication that the terror was, in fact, caused and created by the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when the time comes, I'm going to use this document again. Look what it says in the preamble, particularly the characteristic of the terrain enables this. So the terrain particularly had enabled the BH army to do that, and of course we shall particularly focus on to what extent was true what one of the witnesses stated here before you, that nobody had a monopoly over suffering and equally over terror because it was impossible that in such combat actions and we know who started them, at least during these offensive actions, there was not fear instilled in your own population. This offensive made their own population suffer and, of course, also the population on the other side. So I intend, if you accept, to analyse this document at the right time. This witness explained what he experienced, how this looked like, and that this was exactly how it was, that this was done on a regular basis, destroy and come back. That created enormous hardships for anyone living there, whether it be a Serb or a Muslim, for any living human being. It was plight and suffering, if I may put it, and fear that was permanently there for every living being. This document precisely demonstrates largely, as well as the previous one, that snipers were used for provocation purposes, to shoot at bunkers of the VRS and if you analyse this previous document, then you will see how it was done. You have already admitted that document. This is yet another proof that this was done on the orders of the Supreme Command or the chief of General Staff Rasim Delic, i.e., the highest body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please, sir. Witness, this document is a document stemming from the other side. You, sir, as a witness, when you read this document, the military commander who gave the instruction to his soldiers to act in this manner, he is expecting an action from his subordinates, but is that in order to create destruction, civilian targets, or military targets only? Since you are -- you were a soldier, for one. And secondly, this operation, does it concern civilians or military targets? So as a soldier, I would like you to explain to us this document and I'm going to ask you a subsidiary question, if you will. On the ground you yourself, what did you notice? Did you notice that these orders were implemented, as it stipulates here, or differently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the positions in those parts of town were in houses that were rather dense, these were civilian targets and military targets. A particular case occurred there. This document says that it was aimed at civilians because they killed Sinisa Komjenac's mother then. I knew that she lived there because he was in my platoon, and his mother was there in that apartment, in that red building. That's where his mother lived. They killed her then and he was wounded in the lungs and there was an exchange about 20 days later. So this document proves that there were civilian casualties too. If they were shooting at soldiers, why did they kill this woman?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, an objection, in view of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let's hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry. Allow me to interrupt. It may be necessary for the witness to repeat his answer regarding the body of that woman, because this does not appear in the transcript. I'm looking -- [In English] "There was an exchange about 20 days later." [Interpretation] So this is page 27, line 11. The witness said something else, not an exchange, but he mentioned something else. I don't want to answer instead of him so it might be useful to put the question again to him regarding that body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Please answer, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the speaker because other microphones are on on the Defence side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your microphone is on, so the interpreter is not hearing the speaker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sinisa Komjenac's mother was killed. She stayed on their side and they returned her after some 20 days, through the Commission for Exchanges. There was a state commission for exchanges. There were such commissions on both sides and they communicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Mindua, may I be of assistance? He did mention, when he was speaking a few minutes ago, he mentioned the red building. This red building. Now, who held this red building, in order for this to be clear? And where did the mother live when she got killed in this action? You know, we already discussed that quite a bit, the red building. In this action that is discussed here, in one of these actions, if he could explain to us where this person's mother lived, where, in which part of the building that he mentioned, the red building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be easier to explain with that picture but I can tell you it was on our side. Outside that red building, there was another structure, unoccupied. In the last entranceway they broke out at that location and that's when it happened. From that time on, they held that corner of the red building. It was in their hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is a document which we did not admit because we thought it had been admitted already. In fact it has not. So I'll ask the court deputy to give that a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was the colour photograph of Sarajevo marked by the witness. It was originally P00156 and will be admitted as D218.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: D218. Judge Harhoff has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Elez, I would like to put a question to you in continuation of Judge Mindua's question which you answered earlier, just before the break. And my question is: What do you make of the point number 3 in the order of 11th of July, if we can have that document put back on the screen? The ABiH order of 11th July, signed by commander Rasim Delic. If you see, Mr. Witness, point number 3, are these military targets or are they civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are military targets. Communication network, bridges, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I would agree with you that they are military targets, but this then raises the question of whether this order was complied with by the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Allow me to intervene. The transcript does not reflect what was said by the witness, page 29, line 16 -- or rather 7, because we can see a verb there. And he used a verb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm not sure what -- in the English version, on page 29, line 16, it says that these are military targets. That is the verb.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. [In English] "Communication network, bridges, et cetera." [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... what -- the people who understand B/C/S heard that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's ask the witness. What did you say, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that communication networks, bridges are not military targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So in your view, the order here given by army General Delic was unlawful because he's ordering his troops to attack non-military targets? Is that correctly understood? That is your reading of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, everything you described a few moments ago when you spoke about defence Exhibit 217, namely what happened in the street of Miska Jovanovica in Zagrebacka, where are these streets that you referred to here? Where is Investbanka, where is Mesara, where is Crvena Zgrada, the red building?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: These facilities are on the flanks of Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I know. These attacks came from the flanks. But where are these buildings that I referred to? Where is Zagrebacka street, where is Miska Jovanovica street and notably where is Mesara, Investbanka, the red building, where are they on Grbavica? What kind of buildings are they?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness because of the Defence microphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please turn off your microphone, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These buildings are on the territory under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. These are residential buildings and private homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, could document 3542 be admitted into evidence as a Defence Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D219, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges about something you said? You mentioned that in Ozrenska street, what happened happened to your soldiers, and at one moment you stopped sending soldiers and you refused -- and you refused to be platoon leader, and you no longer wanted to have that possibility of sending someone to those positions. You explained that. However, tell me, please, in this offensive, and particularly during the war, who were all the casualties of this conflict in the area where you were fighting, that is to say in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Ozrenska street, all the houses were private houses. The inhabitants of those houses went out, stood behind their houses, to defend themselves. Many of them lost their lives, and we had to go to send soldiers up there --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Elez, you explained that. You said that as far back as yesterday. Now I'm asking you, during the course of this entire war, particularly during these events that you were talking about now, who were all the casualties in Grbavica? I don't want to say anything else to you. Can you tell me who the victims were and how many victims there were?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody were the victims. Soldiers and civilians. Everybody who lived in Grbavica. I can give you the exact number of soldiers because I was involved with that, as I work in the veterans organisation, and we know exactly how many people got killed, how many soldiers got killed. In the 1st Sarajevo Brigade I can tell you that the number is 608, 608 soldiers. As for civilians, also around 600.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, can you say something else to me? You mentioned sanctions that were imposed roughly, as you said a few moments ago, at the time when General Dragomir Milosevic assumed his duties. Tell me what kind of an effect this had generally speaking on the situation that had to do with living in Grbavica, in every respect, in every respect? I don't want to lead you in any way.

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even before, even before these sanctions, it was hard to live in Grbavica. There wasn't enough food. We lived on humanitarian aid, the entire civilian population and the army. Things were particularly more difficult then for soldiers and civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any difference from a military point of view regarding activities from either side at the time of that offensive and at the time of Dragomir Milosevic's command?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from a military point of view, no. There wasn't any difference. There was always -- it was always hard to live in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any difference in respect of military activities? I'm referring to weapons primarily there.

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards military activities, we felt that the army, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had grown stronger. They were using more shells. We know that they captured some tanks behind Trnovo that they used later. They had communication through the tunnel underneath the airport, so they could bring in weaponry and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I think my time is up and I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Elez.

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Elez, my name is John Docherty. I'm one of the lawyers on the Prosecution side. You and I have not met before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: During the armed conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you were a private soldier except for a spell as a platoon leader; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Can you give us the dates that you began being a platoon leader and the day that you stopped -- the date that you stopped being a platoon leader?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became a platoon leader, I don't know the exact date, and that was in early 1993, and I remained in that position until the end of 1993, so roughly speaking, about a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, as a private soldier, you were a member of a platoon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And that platoon was part of a company?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then what comes next, the battalion, after the company, going up the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And who was the commander -- which battalion were you in and who was its commander?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 2nd Battalion. There were several battalion commanders because one of them was killed, one was wounded, and then another was killed, and actually the third one was just -- let me think for a moment. I do apologise. I know this person very well but I cannot remember his name. Maybe I'll remember -- oh, yes. Anto Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then the battalion was part of the brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Same question as before: Which brigade were you a part of? Who was the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 1st Sarajevo Brigade. The commander was Stojanovic. I think his first name was Veljko.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then finally -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't remember his rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the Prosecutor please turn off the microphone while the witness is speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then finally, above brigade, we reach the corps, which is commanded by the accused, Dragomir Milosevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I want to count the steps, Mr. Elez, between you and the corps commander as we go up the military hierarchy. From platoon to company, that's one step. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Company to battalion makes two, correct?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Battalion to brigade makes three?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And finally brigade to corps makes four steps between you and Dragomir Milosevic, correct?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You spent your entire war in Grbavica, is that right, in the area that you described on your direct examination, along the banks of the Miljacka river?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You did not have any staff duties at the corps level?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Nor were you involved in the day-to-day operations of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, were you?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You don't know what orders, if any, Dragomir Milosevic might have issued to artillery units, do you?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And it would be the same answer, wouldn't it, with regard to snipers within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I don't know. Sniper was not mentioned, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you wouldn't know the workings of the military justice procedures in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, would you, sir? You would not know, for example, under what circumstances an investigation of criminal activity would be opened, would you?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Elez, what was the last job that you had before you entered the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, your last civilian job?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a civilian, I worked at the furniture showroom in Zagrebacka street in Grbavica, and that was in the Sipad company. I was the manager of that showroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And when you did your national service in the Yugoslavian People's Army in 1982, what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a lance corporal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And what sort of work did you do? What were your duties in the JNA in 1982 as a lance corporal?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: My duty in 1992, as a lance corporal, was to train an infantry squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you mean 1982 in that last answer?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in 1982. In the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So at no time, either in the JNA or in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, have you had a position as a commissioned officer with duties for the supervision of a large body of troops; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not an officer, except as when I said I was a platoon commander and a platoon is made up of 20 to 25 troops, and the scope of duty is not very big.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I want to talk with you a little bit, Mr. Elez, about the location of the confrontation lines around the area where you were serving in Grbavica, and could we begin, please, by looking at Defence Exhibit 218? This is a colour photograph that you spent some time marking yesterday, Mr. Elez. Is that on the monitor in front of you, Mr. Elez? Can you see it all right?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When Mr. Tapuskovic asked you where the confrontation line was, you answered verbally that it was the Miljacka river. Do you remember saying that yesterday in response to Mr. Tapuskovic's question?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the Miljacka river.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you drew the red line to show where the -- so show where the confrontation line was. Do you see the red line on the photograph, the one that extends from one side to the other?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That's not on the Miljacka river, is it? The blue line above it is the Miljacka river, correct?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: The blue line is on the other side of the Miljacka. It's not on the Miljacka river. The red line that I put signifies our positions. And between the Miljacka and our positions is some 30 metres. Sometimes 15 metres, sometimes 30 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, then what you are saying, if I understand you correctly, is that the Miljacka river is in between the red line and the blue line? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And Mr. Elez, the reason I'm asking these questions is that the way you drew that red line -- I don't want to testify but it looks like you've put about seven high-rise buildings on your side of the river, on the wrong side, if you will. Do you see what I'm referring to? Is that what you meant to do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, he drew this line and he said where the lines were. This line, as it is, does not mean what the Prosecutor himself, my learned colleague, is interpreting. He put this line and he started explaining it. As it is drawn, it indeed goes through the centre of these buildings. He explained how it all looked like. Therefore, my learned colleague is giving evidence himself and explaining the line. Let him explain the line that he put approximately and let us -- let him tell us what it means. As he put it, he just indicated where they were approximately. The river Miljacka itself could not be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. The witness is to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Elez, do you remember the question or do you need to hear it again?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the question. Allow me to explain why I drew this line in this way. In this picture, it is impossible to put a line adequately because this is a kind of skewed view. If I had a bird eye view I could have drawn it precisely. Allow me to explain going from right to left. On the right-hand side, you see these two high-rise buildings and the line is at the bottom of the building. Someone is better looking at photographs and someone is not so good. Looking at these other high-rise buildings, it's also at the bottom. And this picture doesn't show the distance up to the positions on the Miljacka. You are right, this looks like as if it is before the line, closer to the line.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the last sentence he said?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all these frontal buildings were the positions, except where you see the waterworks buildings. There were no positions there. That's next to the brotherhood and unity bridge or road. It was behind. You also cannot see the garages there. There are lots of facilities and structures that one cannot see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Elez, I fear we are making this more complicated than it needs to be. It's just that the way you drew the line yesterday confused me and I'm trying to make clear by drawing the line there, are you claiming that those buildings, even though they are on your side of the river, were under the control of the ABiH, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or is it just the way you drew the line? Because you didn't have a bird's eye view.

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's how it looks like, because these high-rise buildings are on our side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic is on his feet. When counsel rises, then he has to be heard. What's your point, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is again a suggestion of something that the witness never said, that these buildings, where this line runs through, were on the side of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He never said that. He keeps repeating that these buildings were on the territory of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. He's only now trying to explain this obvious fact. If my colleague Docherty is suggesting that these buildings are on the territory of BH army, the witness never said that, that they were on the territory of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't understand that that was what Mr. Docherty was suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise because I'm -- people are not understanding my questions. I'm just trying to understand what the witness himself says about who had these apartment buildings. And I'm sorry it's turned into such a lengthy process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He has given an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I think so and I'm prepared to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Elez, let's move to a map that you marked yesterday, Defence Exhibit 215 and here I think you had a bird's eye view, if you will. And again, Mr. Elez, do you see the map in front of you? And do you see it clearly?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And here, there is a red line along a main street on the north side of the river. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And that's where you originally put the confrontation line until you were corrected, is that true?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was obviously my big mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you were also asked to draw Mojmilo hill and you drew a large sort of oval-shaped area in the lower left centre of the photograph, is that correct, and labelled it with the letter M, correct?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina controlled Mojmilo hill?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had it under their control. They were deployed on the Mojmilo hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Other witnesses for the Defence in this trial have testified about the drive from Lukavica to Pale along a particular road. Do you see the Lukavica-to-Pale road on this map?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's this yellow line, then I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And do you see that the area you've drawn as Mojmilo hill under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina cuts that road in the lower centre of this map?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see. And this is again my obvious mistake. I am aware that this is a road and this road was not under the control of the BH army. It was under our control. So I stand corrected in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And in fact throughout the war, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps controlled the Lukavica-to-Pale road in its entirety, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all the time. I think not immediately in 1992. This road was cut off several times by the BH army soldiers. They made incursions. It was in the territory under the control of the army of Republika Srpska but there were frequent incursions and fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Were there incursions after 1992? In 1993, 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one incursion. I cannot remember whether it was in 1994 or 1995, because I wasn't up there on the position. I heard that above Zlatiste, the area of Osmica, were infiltrated by the soldiers of the BH army. They wedged themselves into that area. There were a few soldiers of the VRS killed but this area was soon recaptured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And this area was soon recaptured because this road was very important to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, wasn't it? If this road was cut, communications between the barracks in Lukavica and the political leadership in Pale became very, very difficult, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. BH army soldiers couldn't stay there. They just wedged themselves into that area and then they withdrew. That's what I heard. I cannot speak about this because I wasn't there myself on the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, one final question on this point: If there are photographs in evidence in this case taken from the Lukavica-to-Pale road, those photographs are taken from areas under the control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; is that a true statement?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Has it not just been your testimony, Mr. Elez, that except for some incursions that were beaten off, this road was under the control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said. But I didn't understand you about the photographs, your question concerning photographs. Can you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes. If there are photographs in evidence in this case and if those photographs, it is shown, were taken from the Lukavica-to-Pale road - and I don't think you saw any such photographs during your testimony, I don't mean to confuse you - but a photograph taken from the Lukavica-to-Pale road is a photograph taken from an area that, in your testimony, was under the control of the SRK except for some incursions by the army of BH which were beaten off? I apologise. That was a long question but if you understood it, could you tell us whether that's a correct or an incorrect statement?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I still don't understand you. What can be seen in the photographs? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Let me change the question. At the risk of being repetitive, the Lukavica-to-Pale road with the exception of some incursions by the army of BH that were beaten off was under the control of the SRK, true or not true?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I want to cover some of the things that you testified about in your direct examination, and so I'm going to be calling up some of the documents that you looked at already with Mr. Tapuskovic. And could we start, please, with Defence Exhibit 216, 2-1-6? Now, I know this is not terribly easy to read but in your direct examination you said that the shooting referred to in the first paragraph under "our forces," did you tell us what time of day that occurred? It was at 2015 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And that is at 8.15 in the evening, correct?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And this document is -- has a date on it of 15th of October 1994, true?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: On the 15th of October, at 8.15 in the evening, it is dark in Sarajevo, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And this refers to an individual who was, tell me if you agree with this or not, attempting to cross the lines between two opposing armies in the dark.

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, you were, yourself, a private soldier in a trench for a long time, and I'm sure that was a very difficult experience; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You were concerned about your personal safety at all times, true?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is it surprising to you that a person trying to cross the lines during the dark is shot? Is that surprising to you?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That does surprise you?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it surprises me, because a soldier cannot flee from his own army to another. It was probably a civilian and they shot him in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Where in this document, sir, does it say he was shot in the back? Can you point that out to us?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it is stated in the report that a pedestrian is running - I can't see this very well. Can it please be zoomed in - towards the aggressor's side. That is to say from their side to the aggressor's side. It's their report, isn't it? So if he was leaving them, they were probably shooting in his back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So this is a assumption that you make based upon the report? It is not in the report.

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: I get the impression that this is the truth, that at 2015 hours, there was an escapee, that is to say someone escaping from their side, who wanted to cross over to the aggressor's side, and they are calling our side the aggressor's side. That soldier opened fire, as is stated in this report, at that person. Now, was it a civilian or a soldier? Probably a civilian. A soldier never crossed over or fled to the other side. I mean, their soldier. Because at that place, most often it was civilians who were trying to cross over.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And as you said in your last answer, this is their report, meaning this is an army of Bosnia and Herzegovina report, correct?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so after this incident, this report was written, correct?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And this report from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you've just testified, seems to you to be the truth. That is to say, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina shot this man, correct?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably, because this is a report from a soldier to his command. I mean, from the people who were on guard there. Well, there were some cases like that and I believe this is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And this report does not blame the shooting on your side, on the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, does it?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: It takes responsibility for what happened that night, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: There is no claim that this incident has been staged by the Serbian side in order to dirty up the reputation of the Bosnian side, is there, that this was faked, in other words?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Elez, the next topic that I want to cover with you is the incident you described or the occasion you described in your direct testimony when Dragomir Milosevic came to visit your unit on the front lines. You know the occasion that I am referring to; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Do you remember what day that was?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the date. I know it was spring time, because that was the first time I met up with him and talked to him. I have already stated that I met him once. I happened to be there and other soldiers were there too, and that is why I remember this moment. Spring time. I could not remember even the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: General Milosevic had a driver, and I believe he had an aide de camp, a lieutenant. Do you remember the names of those people?

utterances.speaker: Vaso Elez [Resumed]
